Introduction

Linear algebra is a branch of mathematics that studies vectors, vector spaces, and linear transformations between them. It provides a framework for representing and solving systems of linear equations and for describing geometric objects and transformations in a precise mathematical way. The fundamental objects in linear algebra include vectors, matrices, and scalars, which are used to model relationships between quantities.

One of the central ideas of linear algebra is that complex problems can often be expressed as combinations of simpler linear relationships. By organizing data into vectors and matrices, many problems can be solved efficiently using systematic algebraic methods. Concepts such as matrix multiplication, determinants, eigenvalues, and vector spaces form the core tools of this field.

Linear algebra plays a crucial role in many areas of science, engineering, and technology. In computer graphics, it is used to represent and manipulate 2D and 3D objects through transformations such as rotation, scaling, and translation. In machine learning and data science, matrices and vectors are used to represent datasets and perform operations such as regression, dimensionality reduction, and neural network computations. Physics uses linear algebra to describe systems of equations, quantum states, and transformations of physical quantities. It is also fundamental in fields such as signal processing, control systems, economics, and statistics.

Because of its wide applicability, linear algebra is considered one of the most important mathematical foundations for modern computational and scientific work.

Definition: Fields

In linear algebra, vectors are defined over a field. A field is a set of elements together with two operations, usually called addition and multiplication, that satisfy certain rules. These rules ensure that the operations behave similarly to the familiar arithmetic of real numbers.

Typical examples of fields include the real numbers R\mathbb{R}R, the rational numbers Q\mathbb{Q}Q, and the complex numbers C\mathbb{C}C.

Definition: A field FFF is a set equipped with two operations:

  • Addition: +++
  • Multiplication: ⋅\cdot⋅

such that for all a,b,c∈Fa,b,c \in Fa,b,c∈F, the following axioms hold.

Field Axioms: These 9 axioms govern the arithmetic operations in R\mathbb{R}R. We use the quantifiers: ∀\forall∀ (for all / für alle) and ∃\exists∃ (there exists / es existiert).

Associativity (Multiplication) (MA)(x⋅y)⋅z=x⋅(y⋅z)(x\cdot y)\cdot z = x\cdot (y\cdot z)(x⋅y)⋅z=x⋅(y⋅z)∀x,y,z∈R\forall x,y,z \in \mathbb{R}∀x,y,z∈R

Examples of Fields

Natural Numbers N\mathbb{N}N (Not a Field)

The set of natural numbers N={0,1,2,3,… }\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,3,\dots\}N={0,1,2,3,…} is not a field.

Some field axioms are not satisfied:

  • Additive inverse does not exist:
    For example, the additive inverse of 333 would be −3-3−3, but −3∉N-3 \notin \mathbb{N}−3∈/N.

  • Multiplicative inverse does not exist:
    For example, the multiplicative inverse of 222 would be 12\frac{1}{2}21​, but 12∉N\frac{1}{2} \notin \mathbb{N}21​∈/N.

Therefore N\mathbb{N}N does not satisfy the field axioms.

Rational Numbers Q\mathbb{Q}Q

The set of rational numbers

Q={pq∣p,q∈Z, q≠0}\mathbb{Q} = \left\{\frac{p}{q} \mid p,q \in \mathbb{Z},\ q \ne 0 \right\}Q={qp​∣p,q∈Z, q=0}

forms a field.

  • Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (except by zero) are all defined.
  • Every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse.

Example:

35−1=53\frac{3}{5}^{-1} = \frac{5}{3}53​−1=35​

Real Numbers R\mathbb{R}R

The real numbers R\mathbb{R}R also form a field.

They include:

  • rational numbers
  • irrational numbers such as 2\sqrt{2}2​ and π\piπ

All field axioms are satisfied.

Complex Numbers C\mathbb{C}C

The complex numbers

C={a+bi∣a,b∈R, i2=−1}\mathbb{C} = \{a + bi \mid a,b \in \mathbb{R},\ i^2 = -1\}C={a+bi∣a,b∈R, i2=−1}

form a field.

Every non-zero complex number has an inverse:

(a+bi)−1=a−bia2+b2(a+bi)^{-1} = \frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}(a+bi)−1=a2+b2a−bi​

Finite Field Example: Z5\mathbb{Z}_5Z5​

A finite example of a field is the integers modulo 5:

Z5={0,1,2,3,4}\mathbb{Z}_5 = \{0,1,2,3,4\}Z5​={0,1,2,3,4}

Addition and multiplication are performed modulo 5.

Thus Z5\mathbb{Z}_5Z5​ satisfies all field axioms and is a finite field.

In general, Zp\mathbb{Z}_pZp​ is a field whenever ppp is a prime number.

Definition: Vector space

A vector space (or linear space) is a set of elements called vectors together with two operations:

  • vector addition
  • scalar multiplication

The scalars come from a field FFF (for example R\mathbb{R}R or C\mathbb{C}C).

A vector space is denoted by VVV and its elements are vectors v,w,u∈Vv,w,u \in Vv,w,u∈V.

Definition: Let FFF be a field. A vector space over FFF is a set VVV together with

  • a vector addition +:V×V→V+: V \times V \to V+:V×V→V
  • a scalar multiplication ⋅:F×V→V\cdot : F \times V \to V⋅:F×V→V

such that for all u,v,w∈Vu,v,w \in Vu,v,w∈V and all a,b∈Fa,b \in Fa,b∈F the following axioms hold.

Vector Space Axioms

2Commutativity of additionu+v=v+uu + v = v + uu+v=v+u
3Neutral element∃ 0∈V:  v+0=v\exists\,0 \in V:\; v + 0 = v∃0∈V:v+0=v
4Inverse element∀v∈V  ∃(−v)∈V:  v+(−v)=0\forall v \in V\;\exists (-v) \in V:\; v + (-v) = 0∀v∈V∃(−v)∈V:v+(−v)=0

Remarks

  1. The symbols “+” and “·” do not always refer to the same operation in different contexts. Their meaning depends on the structure being considered.

A field is denoted by K\mathbb{K}K (Körper). Operations in a field act on elements of K\mathbb{K}K:

x+Ky∈K,x⋅Ky∈Kx +_{\mathbb{K}} y \in \mathbb{K}, \quad x \cdot_{\mathbb{K}} y \in \mathbb{K}x+K​y∈K,x⋅K​y∈K

Both operations are internal to K\mathbb{K}K.

A vector space VVV is defined over a field K\mathbb{K}K. There are two different operations:

Vector addition:

u+Vv∈Vu +_{V} v \in Vu+V​v∈V

Scalar multiplication:

a⋅K,Vv∈Vwith a∈K,  v∈Va \cdot_{\mathbb{K},V} v \in V \quad \text{with } a \in \mathbb{K},\; v \in Va⋅K,V​v∈Vwith a∈K,v∈V
  1. Uniqueness of the neutral element (Additive identity)

The element 000 is called the zero vector.

Let VVV be a vector space. The neutral element (zero vector) is unique.

Proof:

Assume there exist two neutral elements 0,0′∈V0, 0' \in V0,0′∈V such that for all v∈Vv \in Vv∈V:

v+0=vandv+0′=vv + 0 = v \quad \text{and} \quad v + 0' = vv+0=vandv+0′=v

Now substitute v=0v = 0v=0 into the second equation:

0+0′=00 + 0' = 00+0′=0

Since 000 is a neutral element, we also have:

0+0′=0′0 + 0' = 0'0+0′=0′

Therefore:

0=0′0 = 0'0=0′

Hence, the neutral element is unique.

  1. Uniqueness of additive inverse

The element −v-v−v is called the additive inverse of vvv. Let VVV be a vector space. For every v∈Vv \in Vv∈V, the additive inverse (−v)(-v)(−v) is unique.

Proof:

Assume there exist two additive inverses u,w∈Vu, w \in Vu,w∈V of vvv such that:

v+u=0andv+w=0v + u = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad v + w = 0v+u=0andv+w=0

Then:

u=u+0=u+(v+w)u = u + 0 = u + (v + w)u=u+0=u+(v+w)

By associativity:

u+(v+w)=(u+v)+wu + (v + w) = (u + v) + wu+(v+w)=(u+v)+w

Using u+v=0u + v = 0u+v=0:

(u+v)+w=0+w=w(u + v) + w = 0 + w = w(u+v)+w=0+w=w

Thus:

u=wu = wu=w

Hence the additive inverse is unique.

  1. Interaction with zero vector

Let λ∈K\lambda \in \mathbb{K}λ∈K and x∈Vx \in Vx∈V.

Then:

λ⋅0V=0V\lambda \cdot 0_V = 0_Vλ⋅0V​=0V​

and

0K⋅x=0V0_{\mathbb{K}} \cdot x = 0_V0K​⋅x=0V​

Here:

  • 0V0_V0V​ denotes the zero vector in the vector space VVV
  • 0K0_{\mathbb{K}}0K​ denotes the zero element of the field K\mathbb{K}K

The subscripts distinguish between the zero element of the field and the zero vector in the vector space.

Linear equation in a field

Let a,b∈Ka, b \in \mathbb{K}a,b∈K with a≠0a \neq 0a=0. Consider the equation:

ax+b=0ax + b = 0ax+b=0

Then there exists a unique solution x∈Kx \in \mathbb{K}x∈K given by:

x=−a−1bx = -a^{-1} bx=−a−1b

where:

  • a−1a^{-1}a−1 denotes the multiplicative inverse of aaa

Thus we write:

x=−ba=−a−1bx = -\frac{b}{a} = -a^{-1} bx=−ab​=−a−1b

Examples of vector spaces

  1. A field as a vector space over itself

Every field K\mathbb{K}K is a vector space over itself.

The vector addition and scalar multiplication are simply the field operations:

x+y∈K,λ⋅x∈Kx + y \in \mathbb{K}, \qquad \lambda \cdot x \in \mathbb{K}x+y∈K,λ⋅x∈K

for all x,y,λ∈Kx,y,\lambda \in \mathbb{K}x,y,λ∈K.

Thus the field axioms already guarantee that all vector space axioms are satisfied.

  1. Coordinate vector space Kn\mathbb{K}^nKn

Let K\mathbb{K}K be a field and n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N.

Define

Kn={(x1,x2,…,xn)∣xi∈K, i=1,…,n}\mathbb{K}^n = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) \mid x_i \in \mathbb{K},\ i = 1,\dots,n\}Kn={(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)∣xi​∈K, i=1,…,n}

The operations are defined componentwise.

Vector addition

(x1,x2,…,xn)+(y1,y2,…,yn)=(x1+y1,x2+y2,…,xn+yn)(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) + (y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n) = (x_1 + y_1, x_2 + y_2, \dots, x_n + y_n)(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)+(y1​,y2​,…,yn​)=(x1​+y1​,x2​+y2​,…,xn​+yn​)

Scalar multiplication

λ(x1,x2,…,xn)=(λx1,λx2,…,λxn)\lambda (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) = (\lambda x_1, \lambda x_2, \dots, \lambda x_n)λ(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)=(λx1​,λx2​,…,λxn​)

for λ∈K\lambda \in \mathbb{K}λ∈K.

With these operations, Kn\mathbb{K}^nKn forms a vector space over K\mathbb{K}K.

  1. Function space KM\mathbb{K}^MKM

Let K\mathbb{K}K be a field and MMM a set.

Define

KM={f:M→K}\mathbb{K}^M = \{ f : M \to \mathbb{K} \}KM={f:M→K}

This is the set of all functions from MMM to K\mathbb{K}K.

The operations are defined pointwise.

Vector addition

(f+g)(m)=f(m)+g(m)(f + g)(m) = f(m) + g(m)(f+g)(m)=f(m)+g(m)

Scalar multiplication

(λf)(m)=λ⋅f(m)(\lambda f)(m) = \lambda \cdot f(m)(λf)(m)=λ⋅f(m)

for all m∈Mm \in Mm∈M, f,g∈KMf,g \in \mathbb{K}^Mf,g∈KM, and λ∈K\lambda \in \mathbb{K}λ∈K.

With these operations, KM\mathbb{K}^MKM forms a vector space over K\mathbb{K}K.

Example

Let

M={1,2,3}M = \{1,2,3\}M={1,2,3}

A function f:M→Kf : M \to \mathbb{K}f:M→K is completely determined by

f(1),  f(2),  f(3)f(1),\; f(2),\; f(3)f(1),f(2),f(3)

Thus every function can be written as a tuple

(f(1),f(2),f(3))(f(1), f(2), f(3))(f(1),f(2),f(3))

Therefore

KM≅K3\mathbb{K}^M \cong \mathbb{K}^3KM≅K3

so the function space is equivalent to the coordinate vector space K3\mathbb{K}^3K3.

  1. Polynomial vector space

Let K\mathbb{K}K be a field and n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N.

Let

Pn[x]={p(x)∣p(x) is a polynomial over K with deg⁡(p)≤n}P_n[x] = \{ p(x) \mid p(x) \text{ is a polynomial over } \mathbb{K} \text{ with } \deg(p) \le n \}Pn​[x]={p(x)∣p(x) is a polynomial over K with deg(p)≤n}

be the set of all polynomials with coefficients in K\mathbb{K}K and degree at most nnn.

For p,q∈Pn[x]p,q \in P_n[x]p,q∈Pn​[x] and λ∈K\lambda \in \mathbb{K}λ∈K the operations are defined as:

Polynomial addition

(p+q)(x)=p(x)+q(x)(p + q)(x) = p(x) + q(x)(p+q)(x)=p(x)+q(x)

Scalar multiplication

(λp)(x)=λ⋅p(x)(\lambda p)(x) = \lambda \cdot p(x)(λp)(x)=λ⋅p(x)

With these operations, Pn[x]P_n[x]Pn​[x] forms a vector space over K\mathbb{K}K.

Definition: Subspace

Untervektorraum

Let VVV be a vector space over a field K\mathbb{K}K and let U⊆VU \subseteq VU⊆V.

The subset UUU is called a subspace (Untervektorraum, UVR) of VVV if UUU itself forms a vector space using the same operations as VVV, restricted to UUU.

The operations in VVV are

+:V×V→V+ : V \times V \to V+:V×V→V ⋅:K×V→V\cdot : \mathbb{K} \times V \to V⋅:K×V→V

For UUU to be a subspace, the restricted operations must satisfy

+:U×U→U+ : U \times U \to U+:U×U→U ⋅:K×U→U\cdot : \mathbb{K} \times U \to U⋅:K×U→U

Thus UUU must itself be a vector space over K\mathbb{K}K with these restricted operations.

Characterization of a subspace

Let VVV be a vector space over a field K\mathbb{K}K and let U⊆VU \subseteq VU⊆V.

Then UUU is a subspace of VVV if and only if the following conditions hold:

  1. The zero vector is contained in UUU:
0V∈U0_V \in U0V​∈U
  1. UUU is closed under vector addition:
u,w∈U  ⇒  u+w∈Uu, w \in U \;\Rightarrow\; u + w \in Uu,w∈U⇒u+w∈U
  1. UUU is closed under scalar multiplication:
u∈U, λ∈K  ⇒  λu∈Uu \in U,\ \lambda \in \mathbb{K} \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda u \in Uu∈U, λ∈K⇒λu∈U

If these three properties are satisfied, then UUU forms a vector space over K\mathbb{K}K with the operations inherited from VVV.

Remark

To verify that a subset U⊆VU \subseteq VU⊆V is a subspace, it is sufficient to check the three properties from the characterization above.

In particular, if U⊆VU \subseteq VU⊆V satisfies

  • U≠∅U \neq \emptysetU=∅
  • u,v∈U⇒u+v∈Uu, v \in U \Rightarrow u + v \in Uu,v∈U⇒u+v∈U
  • u∈U, λ∈K⇒λu∈Uu \in U,\ \lambda \in \mathbb{K} \Rightarrow \lambda u \in Uu∈U, λ∈K⇒λu∈U

then UUU is a subspace of VVV.

Equivalently, this can be written as a single closure condition:

u,v∈U, λ,μ∈K  ⇒  λu+μv∈Uu, v \in U,\ \lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{K} \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda u + \mu v \in Uu,v∈U, λ,μ∈K⇒λu+μv∈U

Lemma: Intersection and union of subspaces

Let VVV be a vector space over a field K\mathbb{K}K.

(a) Intersection (Durchschnitt) of subspaces

The intersection of two subspaces of VVV is again a subspace of VVV.

More generally, the intersection of an arbitrary non-empty family of subspaces of VVV is again a subspace.

If (Ui)i∈I(U_i)_{i \in I}(Ui​)i∈I​ is a family of subspaces of VVV, then

⋂i∈IUi\bigcap_{i \in I} U_ii∈I⋂​Ui​

is also a subspace of VVV.

(b) Union (Vereinigung) of subspaces

Let U1U_1U1​ and U2U_2U2​ be subspaces of VVV.

If the union

U1∪U2U_1 \cup U_2U1​∪U2​

is also a subspace of VVV, then one of the subspaces must be contained in the other:

U1⊆U2orU2⊆U1U_1 \subseteq U_2 \quad \text{or} \quad U_2 \subseteq U_1U1​⊆U2​orU2​⊆U1​

Definition: Span

Linear span / lineare Hülle

Let VVV be a vector space over a field K\mathbb{K}K and let M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V.

Consider the family of all subspaces (Untervektorräume) UUU of VVV that contain MMM:

M⊆U⊆VM \subseteq U \subseteq VM⊆U⊆V

This family is not empty, since VVV itself is a subspace containing MMM.

The linear span (lineare Hülle) of MMM is defined as the intersection (Durchschnitt) of all such subspaces:

span⁡(M)=⋂U⊆VU subspaceM⊆UU\operatorname{span}(M) = \bigcap_{\substack{U \subseteq V \\ U \text{ subspace} \\ M \subseteq U}} Uspan(M)=U⊆VU subspaceM⊆U​⋂​U

Thus, span⁡(M)\operatorname{span}(M)span(M) is the smallest subspace of VVV that contains MMM.

We call span⁡(M)\operatorname{span}(M)span(M) the linear span (lineare Hülle) of MMM.

Definition: Linear combination

Linearkombination

Let VVV be a vector space over a field K\mathbb{K}K.

Let

x1,x2,…,xk∈Vx_1, x_2, \dots, x_k \in Vx1​,x2​,…,xk​∈V

and

λ1,λ2,…,λk∈K.\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_k \in \mathbb{K}.λ1​,λ2​,…,λk​∈K.

Then the vector

x=∑i=1kλixix = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i x_ix=i=1∑k​λi​xi​

is called a linear combination (Linearkombination) of the vectors

x1,x2,…,xk.x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k.x1​,x2​,…,xk​.

Here the scalars λ1,…,λk\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_kλ1​,…,λk​ are called the coefficients of the linear combination.

Proposition: Span is all possible linear combinations

Let VVV be a vector space over a field K\mathbb{K}K and let M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V with M≠∅M \neq \emptysetM=∅.

Then the linear span (lineare Hülle) of MMM is exactly the set of all vectors that can be written as linear combinations of vectors from MMM.

That is,

span⁡(M)={∑i=1kλixi  |  k∈N,  xi∈M,  λi∈K}=:W\operatorname{span}(M) = \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i x_i \;\middle|\; k \in \mathbb{N},\; x_i \in M,\; \lambda_i \in \mathbb{K} \right\} =: Wspan(M)={i=1∑k​λi​xi​​k∈N,xi​∈M,λi​∈K}=:W

Thus span⁡(M)\operatorname{span}(M)span(M) consists of all finite linear combinations of vectors from MMM.

Definition: Generating set

Erzeugendes System

Let VVV be a vector space over a field K\mathbb{K}K and let M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V.

We call MMM a generating set (erzeugendes System) of VVV if

span⁡(M)=V.\operatorname{span}(M) = V.span(M)=V.

This means every vector in VVV can be written as a linear combination of vectors in MMM.

If, in addition, no proper subset of MMM is still a generating set of VVV, then MMM is called a minimal generating system (minimales erzeugendes System) of VVV.

Examples

  1. V=R2V = \mathbb{R}^2V=R2

Let V=R2V = \mathbb{R}^2V=R2.

  • The set M2={(1,0),(0,1)}M_2 = \{(1,0), (0,1)\}M2​={(1,0),(0,1)} is a generating set of R2\mathbb{R}^2R2, since every vector (x,y)∈R2(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2(x,y)∈R2 can be written as: (x,y)=x(1,0)+y(0,1)(x,y) = x(1,0) + y(0,1)(x,y)=x(1,0)+y(0,1) Thus, span⁡(M2)=R2\operatorname{span}(M_2) = \mathbb{R}^2span(M2​)=R2.

Moreover, M2M_2M2​ is a minimal generating system.

  1. V=R2V = \mathbb{R}^2V=R2

Let

M3={(2,0),(0,8)}M_3 = \{(2,0), (0,8)\}M3​={(2,0),(0,8)}

Then:

span⁡(M3)={(x,0)∣x∈R}+{(0,y)∣y∈R}=R2\operatorname{span}(M_3) = \{(x,0) \mid x \in \mathbb{R}\} + \{(0,y) \mid y \in \mathbb{R}\} = \mathbb{R}^2span(M3​)={(x,0)∣x∈R}+{(0,y)∣y∈R}=R2

So M3M_3M3​ is a generating set of R2\mathbb{R}^2R2. However, it is not minimal, since scaling does not change the span:

  1. Linear dependence

Let

(2,2)=2(1,1)(2,2) = 2(1,1)(2,2)=2(1,1)

Lemma: Uniqueness of linear combination representation

Lineare Kombination Eindeutigkeit

Let VVV be a vector space over a field K\mathbb{K}K and let M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V.

Let

v=∑i=1kλixiandv=∑i=1kμixiv = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i x_i \quad \text{and} \quad v = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mu_i x_iv=i=1∑k​λi​xi​andv=i=1∑k​μi​xi​

be two representations of the same vector v∈Vv \in Vv∈V, where x1,x2,…,xk∈Mx_1, x_2, \dots, x_k \in Mx1​,x2​,…,xk​∈M are pairwise distinct.

Then it follows that for all i∈{1,2,…,k}i \in \{1,2,\dots,k\}i∈{1,2,…,k}:

λi=μi\lambda_i = \mu_iλi​=μi​

Thus, the coefficients of the linear combination are unique (with respect to a fixed ordered list of linearly independent generators).

Definition: Linear independence

lineare Unabhängigkeit

Let VVV be a vector space over a field K\mathbb{K}K and let k∈Nk \in \mathbb{N}k∈N.

Vectors x1,x2,…,xk∈Vx_1, x_2, \dots, x_k \in Vx1​,x2​,…,xk​∈V are called linearly independent (linear unabhängig) if every linear combination equal to the zero vector is trivial.

That is,

∑i=1kλixi=0  ⇒  λi=0    ∀i∈{1,…,k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i x_i = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_i = 0 \;\; \forall i \in \{1,\dots,k\}i=1∑k​λi​xi​=0⇒λi​=0∀i∈{1,…,k}

Otherwise, the vectors x1,x2,…,xkx_1, x_2, \dots, x_kx1​,x2​,…,xk​ are called linearly dependent (linear abhängig).

Definition: Linear independence of a subset

Let VVV be a vector space and let M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V.

The set MMM is called linear independent if every kkk-tuple of pairwise distinct vectors from MMM, where k∈Nk \in \mathbb{N}k∈N, is linearly independent.

Otherwise, the set MMM is called linear dependent.

In particular, the empty set ∅\emptyset∅ is linear independent.

Remark: Similar to the proof of the lemma, one sees that a subset M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V is linear independent if and only if

∀x∈M:x∉span⁡(M∖{x})\forall x \in M : x \notin \operatorname{span}(M \setminus \{x\})∀x∈M:x∈/span(M∖{x})

That is, no vector in MMM can be written as a linear combination of the other vectors in MMM.

Corollary:

Let M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V.

Then MMM is linear independent if and only if MMM is a minimal generating set for span⁡(M)\operatorname{span}(M)span(M).

That is, MMM generates span⁡(M)\operatorname{span}(M)span(M), and removing any vector from MMM destroys this property.

Theorem: Steinitz Exchange Lemma

Let M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V be a subset, and let

Lu={x1,x2,…,xk}⊆span⁡(M)L_u = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k\} \subseteq \operatorname{span}(M)Lu​={x1​,x2​,…,xk​}⊆span(M)

be a linear independent set with k∈Nk \in \mathbb{N}k∈N.

Then there exist pairwise distinct vectors

y1,y2,…,yk∈My_1, y_2, \dots, y_k \in My1​,y2​,…,yk​∈M

such that

span⁡(M)=span⁡(Lu∪(M∖{y1,y2,…,yk}))\operatorname{span}(M) = \operatorname{span}\bigl(L_u \cup (M \setminus \{y_1, y_2, \dots, y_k\})\bigr)span(M)=span(Lu​∪(M∖{y1​,y2​,…,yk​}))

In particular, MMM contains at least as many elements as LuL_uLu​.

The theorem says:

If you have a set MMM that generates a vector space (or some subspace), and you also have a linear independent set

Lu={x1,x2,…,xk}L_u = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k\}Lu​={x1​,x2​,…,xk​}

whose vectors already lie in span⁡(M)\operatorname{span}(M)span(M), then you can exchange vectors from MMM for the vectors in LuL_uLu​ without changing the span.

More precisely:

  • insert x1,x2,…,xkx_1, x_2, \dots, x_kx1​,x2​,…,xk​ into the generating set,
  • remove exactly kkk suitable vectors y1,y2,…,yky_1, y_2, \dots, y_ky1​,y2​,…,yk​ from MMM,
  • the resulting set still spans exactly the same space.

That is why it is called an exchange lemma.

Intuition: A linear independent set contains no redundant vectors.

So if kkk independent vectors fit inside span⁡(M)\operatorname{span}(M)span(M), then at least kkk vectors in MMM must be replaceable by them.

Hence:

∣Lu∣≤∣M∣|L_u| \leq |M|∣Lu​∣≤∣M∣

So a linearly independent set can never have more vectors than a generating set of the same space.

This is one of the key ideas behind the notion of dimension.

Definition: Basis

Let VVV be a vector space.

A set B⊆VB \subseteq VB⊆V is called a basis of VVV if every vector v∈Vv \in Vv∈V can be written as a linear combination of vectors in BBB, and this representation is unique (i.e. unique up to trivial changes such as adding zero coefficients or reordering terms).

Equivalently: every v∈Vv \in Vv∈V has exactly one set of coefficients (λi)(\lambda_i)(λi​) such that

v=∑b∈Bλb bv = \sum_{b \in B} \lambda_b \, bv=b∈B∑​λb​b

Example

Consider R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 and the standard basis

B={(10),(01)}B = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix} \right\}B={(10​),(01​)}

Let

v=(35)∈R2v = \begin{pmatrix} 3\\ 5 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^2v=(35​)∈R2

Then

v=3(10)+5(01)v = 3 \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} + 5 \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}v=3(10​)+5(01​)

This representation is unique, since no other choice of coefficients produces the same vector.

Hence BBB is a basis of R2\mathbb{R}^2R2.

Corollary: Let VVV be a vector space and let M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V. Then the following statements are equivalent:

a) MMM is a basis of VVV.

b) MMM is linear independent and generates VVV, i.e.

span⁡(M)=V\operatorname{span}(M) = Vspan(M)=V

c) MMM is a maximal linear independent set, i.e. MMM is linear independent and for every v∈V∖Mv \in V \setminus Mv∈V∖M, the set

M∪{v}M \cup \{v\}M∪{v}

is linear dependent.

Definition: Finite-dimensional vector space

We say that a vector space VVV is finite-dimensional and write

dim⁡(V)<∞\dim(V) < \inftydim(V)<∞

if there exists a finite set M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V such that MMM is a basis of VVV (i.e. MMM is a generating set of VVV and linear independent).

Theorem: Let VVV be a finite-dimensional vector space, i.e. dim⁡(V)<∞\dim(V) < \inftydim(V)<∞. Then every linear independent set in VVV (and in particular every basis) is finite, and the following statements hold:

a) Extension to a basis Every linear independent set Lu⊆VL_u \subseteq VLu​⊆V is contained in a basis of VVV, i.e. there exists a basis BBB of VVV such that

Lu⊆BL_u \subseteq BLu​⊆B

b) Subset of a basis in generating sets Every generating set S⊆VS \subseteq VS⊆V contains a basis of VVV, i.e. there exists B⊆SB \subseteq SB⊆S such that BBB is a basis of VVV.

c) Uniqueness of dimension If B1B_1B1​ and B2B_2B2​ are bases of VVV, then

∣B1∣=∣B2∣|B_1| = |B_2|∣B1​∣=∣B2​∣

In particular, all bases of VVV have the same number of elements, called the dimension of VVV.

Corollary: Characterization of a basis

Let VVV be a finite-dimensional vector space, i.e. dim⁡(V)<∞\dim(V) < \inftydim(V)<∞, and let M⊆VM \subseteq VM⊆V.

a) Generating set criterion If MMM is a generating set of VVV and

∣M∣≤dim⁡(V),|M| \leq \dim(V),∣M∣≤dim(V),

then MMM is a basis of VVV.

b) Linear independence criterion If MMM is linear independent and

∣M∣≥dim⁡(V),|M| \geq \dim(V),∣M∣≥dim(V),

then MMM is a basis of VVV.

Lemma: Dimension of subspaces

Let VVV be a finite-dimensional vector space, i.e. dim⁡(V)<∞\dim(V) < \inftydim(V)<∞, and let U⊆VU \subseteq VU⊆V be a subspace.

Then

dim⁡(U)≤dim⁡(V)\dim(U) \leq \dim(V)dim(U)≤dim(V)

Moreover,

dim⁡(U)=dim⁡(V)⟺U=V\dim(U) = \dim(V) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad U = Vdim(U)=dim(V)⟺U=V

In words: a subspace cannot have larger dimension than the whole space, and it has the same dimension only if it is the whole space.

Example: Polynomial vector space R[x]\mathbb{R}[x]R[x]

Consider the vector space R[x]\mathbb{R}[x]R[x] of all real-valued polynomials

p(x)=a0+a1x+a2x2+⋯+anxnp(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \cdots + a_n x^np(x)=a0​+a1​x+a2​x2+⋯+an​xn

with ai∈Ra_i \in \mathbb{R}ai​∈R.

Define the set

{1,x,x2,x3,… }={xk∣k∈N0}\{1, x, x^2, x^3, \dots\} = \{x^k \mid k \in \mathbb{N}_0\}{1,x,x2,x3,…}={xk∣k∈N0​}

Claim This set is linear independent.

Proof idea

Assume a finite linear combination equals the zero polynomial:

λ0⋅1+λ1x+λ2x2+⋯+λnxn=0\lambda_0 \cdot 1 + \lambda_1 x + \lambda_2 x^2 + \cdots + \lambda_n x^n = 0λ0​⋅1+λ1​x+λ2​x2+⋯+λn​xn=0

This means the polynomial is the zero function, i.e. it is zero for all x∈Rx \in \mathbb{R}x∈R.

A polynomial is identically zero if and only if all coefficients are zero. Hence

λ0=λ1=⋯=λn=0\lambda_0 = \lambda_1 = \cdots = \lambda_n = 0λ0​=λ1​=⋯=λn​=0

Therefore the only solution is the trivial one, so {1,x,x2,… }\{1, x, x^2, \dots\}{1,x,x2,…} is linear independent.

Definition: Sum of subsets

Let VVV be a vector space, n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N, and let M1,M2,…,Mn⊆VM_1, M_2, \dots, M_n \subseteq VM1​,M2​,…,Mn​⊆V.

The sum of these sets is defined as

M1+M2+⋯+Mn:={∑k=1nxk  |  xk∈Mk for k=1,…,n}M_1 + M_2 + \cdots + M_n := \left\{ \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k \;\middle|\; x_k \in M_k \text{ for } k=1,\dots,n \right\}M1​+M2​+⋯+Mn​:={k=1∑n​xk​​xk​∈Mk​ for k=1,…,n}

This construction is called the sum of subsets (or simply set sum).
In more general contexts, it is also known as the Minkowski sum.

Example

Let V=R2V = \mathbb{R}^2V=R2 and consider

M1={(1,0),(0,1)},M2={(1,1)}M_1 = \{(1,0), (0,1)\}, \qquad M_2 = \{(1,1)\}M1​={(1,0),(0,1)},M2​={(1,1)}

Then

M1+M2={x+y∣x∈M1,y∈M2}M_1 + M_2 = \{x + y \mid x \in M_1, y \in M_2\}M1​+M2​={x+y∣x∈M1​,y∈M2​}

Compute all combinations:

  • (1,0)+(1,1)=(2,1)(1,0) + (1,1) = (2,1)(1,0)+(1,1)=(2,1)
  • (0,1)+(1,1)=(1,2)(0,1) + (1,1) = (1,2)(0,1)+(1,1)=(1,2)

So

M1+M2={(2,1),(1,2)}M_1 + M_2 = \{(2,1), (1,2)\}M1​+M2​={(2,1),(1,2)}

Lemma

Let VVV be a vector space.

a) Associativity of set addition For subspaces M1,M2,M3⊆VM_1, M_2, M_3 \subseteq VM1​,M2​,M3​⊆V it holds that

M1+M2+M3=(M1+M2)+M3M_1 + M_2 + M_3 = (M_1 + M_2) + M_3M1​+M2​+M3​=(M1​+M2​)+M3​

b) Cosets of a subspace

Let U⊆VU \subseteq VU⊆V be a subspace and let x,y∈Vx, y \in Vx,y∈V.
We use the abbreviation

U+z:=U+{z}for z∈VU + z := U + \{z\} \quad \text{for } z \in VU+z:=U+{z}for z∈V

Then the following equivalence holds:

U+x=U+yU + x = U + yU+x=U+y

if and only if

(U+x)∩(U+y)≠∅(U + x) \cap (U + y) \neq \emptyset(U+x)∩(U+y)=∅

if and only if

x−y∈Ux - y \in Ux−y∈U

c) Sum of subspaces and linear hull

Let v1,v2∈Vv_1, v_2 \in Vv1​,v2​∈V and let U⊆VU \subseteq VU⊆V be a subspace. Then

span⁡({v1,v2})={v1}+{v2}\operatorname{span}(\{v_1, v_2\}) = \{v_1\} + \{v_2\}span({v1​,v2​})={v1​}+{v2​}

In particular, the sum of subspaces is again a subspace.

Definition: Direct Sum

direkte Summe

Let VVV be a vector space, let n∈Nn \in \mathbb{N}n∈N, and let

V1,V2,…,VnV_1, V_2, \dots, V_nV1​,V2​,…,Vn​

be subspaces of VVV.

We say that VVV is the direct sum of the subspaces ViV_iVi​ and write

V=V1⊕V2⊕⋯⊕Vn=⨁i=1nViV = V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus V_n = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{n} V_iV=V1​⊕V2​⊕⋯⊕Vn​=i=1⨁n​Vi​

if

V=V1+V2+⋯+VnV = V_1 + V_2 + \cdots + V_nV=V1​+V2​+⋯+Vn​

and for all vectors

xi∈Vi(i=1,…,n)x_i \in V_i \qquad (i = 1, \dots, n)xi​∈Vi​(i=1,…,n)

the implication

∑i=1nxi=0⟹x1=x2=⋯=xn=0\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n = 0i=1∑n​xi​=0⟹x1​=x2​=⋯=xn​=0

holds.

In other words, every vector in VVV has a unique representation as a sum of vectors from the subspaces ViV_iVi​.

Why Do We Need the Direct Sum?

The ordinary sum of subspaces

V1+V2V_1 + V_2V1​+V2​

only tells us that every vector can be written as

v=v1+v2(v1∈V1,  v2∈V2)v = v_1 + v_2 \qquad (v_1 \in V_1,\; v_2 \in V_2)v=v1​+v2​(v1​∈V1​,v2​∈V2​)

However, this representation is not necessarily unique.

The direct sum adds the important condition of uniqueness.

Ordinary Sum vs Direct Sum

Ordinary Sum

For subspaces V1,V2⊆VV_1, V_2 \subseteq VV1​,V2​⊆V,

V1+V2={v1+v2∣v1∈V1,  v2∈V2}V_1 + V_2 = \{v_1 + v_2 \mid v_1 \in V_1,\; v_2 \in V_2\}V1​+V2​={v1​+v2​∣v1​∈V1​,v2​∈V2​}

means:

  • every vector can be expressed as a sum,
  • but possibly in many different ways.

Direct Sum

The notation

V=V1⊕V2V = V_1 \oplus V_2V=V1​⊕V2​

means:

  1. every vector in VVV can be written as

    v=v1+v2v = v_1 + v_2v=v1​+v2​

  2. this decomposition is unique.

Equivalently,

V1∩V2={0}V_1 \cap V_2 = \{0\}V1​∩V2​={0}

Example: Not a Direct Sum

Let

V1=span⁡{(1,0)}V_1 = \operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}V1​=span{(1,0)}

and

V2=span⁡{(1,0)}V_2 = \operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}V2​=span{(1,0)}

inside R2\mathbb{R}^2R2.

Then

V1+V2=V1V_1 + V_2 = V_1V1​+V2​=V1​

but this is not a direct sum because

V1∩V2=V1≠{0}V_1 \cap V_2 = V_1 \neq \{0\}V1​∩V2​=V1​={0}

The zero vector can be written in many ways:

0=(1,0)+(−1,0)0 = (1,0) + (-1,0)0=(1,0)+(−1,0)

with nonzero vectors from the two spaces.

So the decomposition is not unique.

Example: Direct Sum

Let

V1=span⁡{(1,0)},V2=span⁡{(0,1)}V_1 = \operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}, \qquad V_2 = \operatorname{span}\{(0,1)\}V1​=span{(1,0)},V2​=span{(0,1)}

Then

R2=V1⊕V2\mathbb{R}^2 = V_1 \oplus V_2R2=V1​⊕V2​

because every vector

(a,b)(a,b)(a,b)

has the unique decomposition

(a,b)=(a,0)+(0,b)(a,b) = (a,0) + (0,b)(a,b)=(a,0)+(0,b)

and

V1∩V2={0}V_1 \cap V_2 = \{0\}V1​∩V2​={0}

Direct sums allow us to:

  • split vector spaces into independent parts,
  • work with coordinates uniquely,
  • simplify linear maps and matrices,
  • decompose spaces into simpler subspaces,
  • define bases and dimensions cleanly.

They appear everywhere in linear algebra, for example:

  • eigenspaces,
  • orthogonal decompositions,
  • Fourier series,
  • diagonalization,
  • module theory,
  • functional analysis.

The direct sum is essentially the vector-space version of combining independent components.

Example

Consider the subspaces of R2\mathbb{R}^2R2

V1=span⁡{(1,0)},V2=span⁡{(0,1)}V_1 = \operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}, \qquad V_2 = \operatorname{span}\{(0,1)\}V1​=span{(1,0)},V2​=span{(0,1)}

Then every vector (a,b)∈R2(a,b) \in \mathbb{R}^2(a,b)∈R2 can be written uniquely as

(a,b)=(a,0)+(0,b)(a,b) = (a,0) + (0,b)(a,b)=(a,0)+(0,b)

with

(a,0)∈V1,(0,b)∈V2(a,0) \in V_1, \qquad (0,b) \in V_2(a,0)∈V1​,(0,b)∈V2​

Hence,

R2=V1⊕V2\mathbb{R}^2 = V_1 \oplus V_2R2=V1​⊕V2​

Lemma: Union of Linearly Independent Sets

Let VVV be a vector space over a field KKK and let

L1,L2⊆VL_1, L_2 \subseteq VL1​,L2​⊆V

be linearly independent sets with

L1∩L2=∅L_1 \cap L_2 = \emptysetL1​∩L2​=∅

Then

L1∪L2 is linearly independent  ⟺  span⁡(L1)∩span⁡(L2)={0}L_1 \cup L_2 \text{ is linearly independent} \iff \operatorname{span}(L_1) \cap \operatorname{span}(L_2) = \{0\}L1​∪L2​ is linearly independent⟺span(L1​)∩span(L2​)={0}

v=∑i=1maixi=∑j=1nbjyjv = \sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i x_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} b_j y_jv=i=1∑m​ai​xi​=j=1∑n​bj​yj​

with

xi∈L1,yj∈L2x_i \in L_1, \qquad y_j \in L_2xi​∈L1​,yj​∈L2​

Hence

∑i=1maixi−∑j=1nbjyj=0\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i x_i - \sum_{j=1}^{n} b_j y_j = 0i=1∑m​ai​xi​−j=1∑n​bj​yj​=0

Since L1∪L2L_1 \cup L_2L1​∪L2​ is linearly independent, all coefficients vanish. Thus

v=0v = 0v=0

Therefore,

span⁡(L1)∩span⁡(L2)={0}\operatorname{span}(L_1) \cap \operatorname{span}(L_2) = \{0\}span(L1​)∩span(L2​)={0}

"⇐\Leftarrow⇐"

Assume

span⁡(L1)∩span⁡(L2)={0}\operatorname{span}(L_1) \cap \operatorname{span}(L_2) = \{0\}span(L1​)∩span(L2​)={0}

and let

∑i=1maixi+∑j=1nbjyj=0\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i x_i + \sum_{j=1}^{n} b_j y_j = 0i=1∑m​ai​xi​+j=1∑n​bj​yj​=0

with

xi∈L1,yj∈L2x_i \in L_1, \qquad y_j \in L_2xi​∈L1​,yj​∈L2​

Then

∑i=1maixi=−∑j=1nbjyj\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i x_i = - \sum_{j=1}^{n} b_j y_ji=1∑m​ai​xi​=−j=1∑n​bj​yj​

The left-hand side lies in span⁡(L1)\operatorname{span}(L_1)span(L1​) and the right-hand side in span⁡(L2)\operatorname{span}(L_2)span(L2​), hence both are 000.

Since L1L_1L1​ and L2L_2L2​ are linearly independent, all coefficients vanish. Therefore,

L1∪L2L_1 \cup L_2L1​∪L2​

is linearly independent.

Corollary: Criterion for a Direct Sum

Let VVV be a vector space and let

V1,V2⊆VV_1, V_2 \subseteq VV1​,V2​⊆V

be subspaces.

Then

V1+V2=V1⊕V2  ⟺  V1∩V2={0}V_1 + V_2 = V_1 \oplus V_2 \iff V_1 \cap V_2 = \{0\}V1​+V2​=V1​⊕V2​⟺V1​∩V2​={0}
- The field element $1$ is the **multiplicative identity** of $F$.

Definition: Linear Maps

lineare Abbildungen

Let XXX and VVV be vector spaces over a field KKK.

A map

f:X→Vf : X \to Vf:X→V

is called a KKK-linear map if for all

x,y∈X,λ∈Kx, y \in X, \qquad \lambda \in Kx,y∈X,λ∈K

the relation

f(λx+y)=λf(x)+f(y)f(\lambda x + y) = \lambda f(x) + f(y)f(λx+y)=λf(x)+f(y)

holds.

We denote by

Lin⁡K(X,V)\operatorname{Lin}_K(X,V)LinK​(X,V)

the set of all linear maps from XXX to VVV.

If the field KKK is clear from the context, we also write

Lin⁡(X,V)\operatorname{Lin}(X,V)Lin(X,V)

Example: A Map That Is Not Linear

Consider the map

f:R→R,f(x)=4x+7f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad f(x) = 4x + 7f:R→R,f(x)=4x+7

We check the linearity condition:

f(λx+y)=4(λx+y)+7=4λx+4y+7f(\lambda x + y) = 4(\lambda x + y) + 7 = 4\lambda x + 4y + 7f(λx+y)=4(λx+y)+7=4λx+4y+7

On the other hand,

λf(x)+f(y)=λ(4x+7)+(4y+7)=4λx+7λ+4y+7\lambda f(x) + f(y) = \lambda(4x + 7) + (4y + 7) = 4\lambda x + 7\lambda + 4y + 7λf(x)+f(y)=λ(4x+7)+(4y+7)=4λx+7λ+4y+7

In general,

4λx+4y+7≠4λx+7λ+4y+74\lambda x + 4y + 7 \neq 4\lambda x + 7\lambda + 4y + 74λx+4y+7=4λx+7λ+4y+7

Hence,

f(λx+y)≠λf(x)+f(y)f(\lambda x + y) \neq \lambda f(x) + f(y)f(λx+y)=λf(x)+f(y)

Therefore, fff is not linear.

The problem is the constant term 777.

Linear maps must satisfy

f(0)=0f(0) = 0f(0)=0

but here

f(0)=7≠0f(0) = 7 \neq 0f(0)=7=0

Remark

A map

f:X→Yf : X \to Yf:X→Y

is linear

  ⟺  {f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)f(λx)=λf(x)∀x,y∈X, λ∈K\iff \begin{cases} f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) \\ f(\lambda x) = \lambda f(x) \end{cases} \quad \forall x,y \in X,\ \lambda \in K⟺{f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)f(λx)=λf(x)​∀x,y∈X, λ∈K

In particular,

f(0)=0f(0) = 0f(0)=0

since

f(0)=f(0+0)=f(0)+f(0)  ⇒  f(0)=0f(0) = f(0+0) = f(0) + f(0) \;\Rightarrow\; f(0)=0f(0)=f(0+0)=f(0)+f(0)⇒f(0)=0

Remark: Graph of a Linear Map

Let f:X→Vf : X \to Vf:X→V. Then

f is linear⟺gr⁡(f)⊆X×V is a subspacef \text{ is linear} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \operatorname{gr}(f) \subseteq X \times V \text{ is a subspace}f is linear⟺gr(f)⊆X×V is a subspace

where the graph is defined as

gr⁡(f)={(x,f(x))∣x∈X}⊆X×V\operatorname{gr}(f) = \{(x, f(x)) \mid x \in X\} \subseteq X \times Vgr(f)={(x,f(x))∣x∈X}⊆X×V

The vector space structure on X×VX \times VX×V is given by

(x1,v1)+(x2,v2)=(x1+x2,v1+v2)(x_1, v_1) + (x_2, v_2) = (x_1 + x_2, v_1 + v_2)(x1​,v1​)+(x2​,v2​)=(x1​+x2​,v1​+v2​)

and

λ(x,v)=(λx,λv)\lambda (x, v) = (\lambda x, \lambda v)λ(x,v)=(λx,λv)

for all x,x1,x2∈Xx, x_1, x_2 \in Xx,x1​,x2​∈X, v,v1,v2∈Vv, v_1, v_2 \in Vv,v1​,v2​∈V, and λ∈K\lambda \in Kλ∈K.

Thus, linearity of fff is equivalent to saying that its graph is closed under addition and scalar multiplication in X×VX \times VX×V.

Example

Let

f:R2→R,f(u,v)=u+vf : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad f(u,v) = u + vf:R2→R,f(u,v)=u+v

We check linearity.

Additivity

For (u1,v1),(u2,v2)∈R2(u_1,v_1), (u_2,v_2) \in \mathbb{R}^2(u1​,v1​),(u2​,v2​)∈R2:

f((u1,v1)+(u2,v2))=f(u1+u2,  v1+v2)=(u1+u2)+(v1+v2)=u1+v1+u2+v2f\big((u_1,v_1) + (u_2,v_2)\big) = f(u_1+u_2,\; v_1+v_2) = (u_1+u_2) + (v_1+v_2) = u_1 + v_1 + u_2 + v_2f((u1​,v1​)+(u2​,v2​))=f(u1​+u2​,v1​+v2​)=(u1​+u2​)+(v1​+v2​)=u1​+v1​+u2​+v2​

On the other hand:

f(u1,v1)+f(u2,v2)=(u1+v1)+(u2+v2)=u1+v1+u2+v2f(u_1,v_1) + f(u_2,v_2) = (u_1+v_1) + (u_2+v_2) = u_1 + v_1 + u_2 + v_2f(u1​,v1​)+f(u2​,v2​)=(u1​+v1​)+(u2​+v2​)=u1​+v1​+u2​+v2​

So additivity holds.

Homogeneity

For λ∈R\lambda \in \mathbb{R}λ∈R:

f(λ(u,v))=f(λu,λv)=λu+λv=λ(u+v)=λf(u,v)f(\lambda (u,v)) = f(\lambda u, \lambda v) = \lambda u + \lambda v = \lambda (u+v) = \lambda f(u,v)f(λ(u,v))=f(λu,λv)=λu+λv=λ(u+v)=λf(u,v)

Conclusion

f is linear.f \text{ is linear.}f is linear.

Definition: Image and Kernel

Let

Image

im⁡(f)=f(X)={f(x)∣x∈X}⊆V\operatorname{im}(f) = f(X) = \{ f(x) \mid x \in X \} \subseteq Vim(f)=f(X)={f(x)∣x∈X}⊆V

Kernel

Kern

ker⁡(f)={x∈X∣f(x)=0}⊆X\ker(f) = \{ x \in X \mid f(x) = 0 \} \subseteq Xker(f)={x∈X∣f(x)=0}⊆X

If fff is linear, then:

Lemma: Image, Kernel and Injectivity

Let

f:X→Vf : X \to Vf:X→V

be a linear map.

Then:

a) Subspace properties

im⁡(f)≤V,ker⁡(f)≤X\operatorname{im}(f) \le V, \qquad \ker(f) \le Xim(f)≤V,ker(f)≤X

i.e. both the image and the kernel are subspaces.

b) Injectivity criterion

f is injective  ⟺  ker⁡(f)={0}f \text{ is injective} \iff \ker(f) = \{0\}f is injective⟺ker(f)={0}

c) Structure of preimages

For all x∈Xx \in Xx∈X:

f−1(f(x))=x+ker⁡(f)f^{-1}(f(x)) = x + \ker(f)f−1(f(x))=x+ker(f)

i.e.

f−1(f(x))={x+k∣k∈ker⁡(f)}f^{-1}(f(x)) = \{x + k \mid k \in \ker(f)\}f−1(f(x))={x+k∣k∈ker(f)}

d) Existence of a Left Inverse

If

g:im⁡(f)→Xg : \operatorname{im}(f) \to Xg:im(f)→X

satisfies

g(f(x))=xfor all x∈X,g(f(x)) = x \qquad \text{for all } x \in X,g(f(x))=xfor all x∈X,

then

g∈Lin⁡(im⁡(f),X).g \in \operatorname{Lin}(\operatorname{im}(f), X).g∈Lin(im(f),X).

Such a map ( g ) exists if and only if ( f ) is injective.

From (a) it follows that

f is surjective  ⟺  im⁡(f)=V.f \text{ is surjective} \iff \operatorname{im}(f) = V.f is surjective⟺im(f)=V.

Indeed, let

v∈V.v \in V.v∈V.

If

v=∑i=1nλivi,vi∈im⁡(f),v = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i v_i, \qquad v_i \in \operatorname{im}(f),v=i=1∑n​λi​vi​,vi​∈im(f),

and

vi=f(xi),v_i = f(x_i),vi​=f(xi​),

then

v=∑i=1nλif(xi)=∑i=1nf(λixi)=f(∑i=1nλixi).v = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i f(x_i) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(\lambda_i x_i) = f\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i x_i \right).v=i=1∑n​λi​f(xi​)=i=1∑n​f(λi​xi​)=f(i=1∑n​λi​xi​).

Proof

Let

x1,x2∈ker⁡(f).x_1, x_2 \in \ker(f).x1​,x2​∈ker(f).

Then

f(x1+x2)=f(x1)+f(x2)=0+0=0.f(x_1 + x_2) = f(x_1) + f(x_2) = 0 + 0 = 0.f(x1​+x2​)=f(x1​)+f(x2​)=0+0=0.

Hence,

x1+x2∈ker⁡(f).x_1 + x_2 \in \ker(f).x1​+x2​∈ker(f).

Now let

λ∈K\lambda \in Kλ∈K

and

x∈ker⁡(f).x \in \ker(f).x∈ker(f).

Then

f(λx)=λf(x)=λ⋅0=0.f(\lambda x) = \lambda f(x) = \lambda \cdot 0 = 0.f(λx)=λf(x)=λ⋅0=0.

Therefore,

λx∈ker⁡(f).\lambda x \in \ker(f).λx∈ker(f). ker⁡(f)≤X.\ker(f) \le X.ker(f)≤X.

Definition: Rank and Nullity

Definition: Rang und Defekt

Let

f∈Lin⁡(X,V).f \in \operatorname{Lin}(X, V).f∈Lin(X,V).

Then we define

rank⁡(f):=dim⁡(im⁡(f))\operatorname{rank}(f) := \dim(\operatorname{im}(f))rank(f):=dim(im(f))

to be the rank of (f), and

nullity⁡(f):=dim⁡(ker⁡(f))\operatorname{nullity}(f) := \dim(\ker(f))nullity(f):=dim(ker(f))

to be the nullity of (f).

Theorem: Rank–Nullity Theorem

Satz: Rang–Defekt–Formel

Let

f∈Lin⁡(X,V)f \in \operatorname{Lin}(X, V)f∈Lin(X,V)

with

dim⁡(X)<∞.\dim(X) < \infty.dim(X)<∞.

Then

dim⁡(X)=dim⁡(im⁡(f))+dim⁡(ker⁡(f))\dim(X) = \dim(\operatorname{im}(f)) + \dim(\ker(f))dim(X)=dim(im(f))+dim(ker(f))

i.e.

dim⁡(X)=rank⁡(f)+nullity⁡(f).\dim(X) = \operatorname{rank}(f) + \operatorname{nullity}(f).dim(X)=rank(f)+nullity(f).

In particular, if

dim⁡(X)=dim⁡(V),\dim(X) = \dim(V),dim(X)=dim(V),

then

f is bijective  ⟺  f is injective  ⟺  f is surjective.f \text{ is bijective} \iff f \text{ is injective} \iff f \text{ is surjective}.f is bijective⟺f is injective⟺f is surjective.

Definition: Matrices

Definition: Matrizen

Let

m,n∈N.m, n \in \mathbb{N}.m,n∈N.

An m×nm \times nm×n-matrix over KKK is a mapping

a:{1,…,m}×{1,…,n}→Ka : \{1, \dots, m\} \times \{1, \dots, n\} \to Ka:{1,…,m}×{1,…,n}→K

Km×nK^{m \times n}Km×n

A=(a11⋯a1n⋮⋱⋮am1⋯amn).A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & \cdots & a_{1n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_{m1} & \cdots & a_{mn} \end{pmatrix}.A=​a11​⋮am1​​⋯⋱⋯​a1n​⋮amn​​​.

The iii-th row is given by

Ai,⋅=(ai1,ai2,…,ain)∈Kn,i∈{1,…,m}.A_{i,\cdot} = (a_{i1}, a_{i2}, \dots, a_{in}) \in K^n, \qquad i \in \{1, \dots, m\}.Ai,⋅​=(ai1​,ai2​,…,ain​)∈Kn,i∈{1,…,m}.

The jjj-th column is given by

A⋅,j=(a1j⋮amj)∈Km,j∈{1,…,n}.A_{\cdot,j} = \begin{pmatrix} a_{1j} \\ \vdots \\ a_{mj} \end{pmatrix} \in K^m, \qquad j \in \{1, \dots, n\}.A⋅,j​=​a1j​⋮amj​​​∈Km,j∈{1,…,n}.

Matrix operations and associated linear map

Km×nK^{m \times n}Km×n: Addition and scalar multiplication

On Km×nK^{m \times n}Km×n we define:

Addition

(a+b)ij=aij+bij,(i,j)∈{1,…,m}×{1,…,n}.(a + b)_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij}, \qquad (i,j) \in \{1,\dots,m\} \times \{1,\dots,n\}.(a+b)ij​=aij​+bij​,(i,j)∈{1,…,m}×{1,…,n}.

(λ⋅a)ij=λaij.(\lambda \cdot a)_{ij} = \lambda a_{ij}.(λ⋅a)ij​=λaij​.

Lemma: Equivalence of Invertibility and Full Rank

Matrix as a Mapping
Formally, a matrix A∈Km×nA \in K^{m \times n}A∈Km×n can be rigorously defined as a function that maps pairs of indices to elements of a scalar field KKK:

A:{1,…,m}×{1,…,n}→KA: \{1, \dots, m\} \times \{1, \dots, n\} \to KA:{1,…,m}×{1,…,n}→K (i,j)↦A(i,j)=aij(i, j) \mapsto A(i, j) = a_{ij}(i,j)↦A(i,j)=aij​

In standard tabular form, we write this function out as:

A=(a11…a1n⋮⋱⋮am1…amn)A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & \dots & a_{1n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_{m1} & \dots & a_{mn} \end{pmatrix}A=​a11​⋮am1​​…⋱…​a1n​⋮amn​​​

The Induced Linear Map
Every matrix A∈Km×nA \in K^{m \times n}A∈Km×n defines a canonical matrix transformation TA:Kn→KmT_A: K^n \to K^mTA​:Kn→Km via left-multiplication:

TA(x)=AxT_A(x) = AxTA​(x)=Ax

This mapping respects the algebraic structure of vector spaces. Its linearity is demonstrated via the distributive property of matrix multiplication over vector addition (additivity):

TA(x+y)=A(x+y)=Ax+Ay=TA(x)+TA(y)T_A(x + y) = A(x + y) = Ax + Ay = T_A(x) + T_A(y)TA​(x+y)=A(x+y)=Ax+Ay=TA​(x)+TA​(y)

Lemma

Let A∈Kn×nA \in K^{n \times n}A∈Kn×n be a square matrix. The following statements are equivalent:

  • (a) The inverse matrix A−1A^{-1}A−1 exists (i.e., AAA is regular/invertible).
  • (b) rank(A)=n\text{rank}(A) = nrank(A)=n (i.e., AAA has full rank, meaning the induced linear map TA:Kn→KnT_A: K^n \to K^nTA​:Kn→Kn is bijective).

Remarks on Matrix Properties and Non-Commutativity

(a) Functional vs. Matrix Definitions
Geometric and algebraic properties like injectivity, surjectivity, or the existence of an inverse mapping (∘−1\circ^{-1}∘−1) are fundamentally defined for functions (such as linear transformations TAT_ATA​). They are not intrinsically defined for a static grid of numbers (a matrix AAA). However, we naturally extend these definitions to matrices via the canonical induced mapping TA:Kn→KmT_A: K^n \to K^mTA​:Kn→Km.

(b) Non-Commutativity of Matrix Multiplication
Unlike scalar multiplication in the field KKK, matrix multiplication is generally non-commutative. Even for square matrices of the same dimension where both products ABABAB and BABABA are well-defined, AB≠BAAB \neq BAAB=BA in most cases.

Counterexample (2×22 \times 22×2 Matrices) To demonstrate non-commutativity, consider the following two matrices in K2×2K^{2 \times 2}K2×2:

A=(1000),B=(0100)A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}A=(10​00​),B=(00​10​)

Computing the product ABABAB:

AB=(1000)(0100)=(1⋅0+0⋅01⋅1+0⋅00⋅0+0⋅00⋅1+0⋅0)=(0100)AB = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1\cdot0 + 0\cdot0 & 1\cdot1 + 0\cdot0 \\ 0\cdot0 + 0\cdot0 & 0\cdot1 + 0\cdot0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}AB=(10​00​)(00​10​)=(1⋅0+0⋅00⋅0+0⋅0​1⋅1+0⋅00⋅1+0⋅0​)=(00​10​)

Computing the product BABABA:

BA=(0100)(1000)=(0⋅1+1⋅00⋅0+1⋅00⋅1+0⋅00⋅0+0⋅0)=(0000)BA = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0\cdot1 + 1\cdot0 & 0\cdot0 + 1\cdot0 \\ 0\cdot1 + 0\cdot0 & 0\cdot0 + 0\cdot0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}BA=(00​10​)(10​00​)=(0⋅1+1⋅00⋅1+0⋅0​0⋅0+1⋅00⋅0+0⋅0​)=(00​00​)

Since AB≠BAAB \neq BAAB=BA, order matters.

Algebraic Criteria for the Inverse Matrix

In general algebraic structures (like monoids), showing that an element is an inverse requires verifying both the left-inverse and right-inverse properties independently. However, for square matrices over a field KKK, a one-sided inverse is automatically a two-sided inverse.

Lemma (One-Sided Inverse Sufficiency)

Let A,B∈Kn×nA, B \in K^{n \times n}A,B∈Kn×n be square matrices. The matrix BBB is the unique inverse of AAA (denoted B=A−1B = A^{-1}B=A−1) if and only if any of the following equivalent conditions hold:

B=A−1  ⟺  AB=In  ⟺  BA=InB = A^{-1} \iff AB = I_n \iff BA = I_nB=A−1⟺AB=In​⟺BA=In​

_(where InI_nIn​ denotes the n×nn \times nn×n identity matrix idKn\text{id}_{K^n}idKn​)_

Method: Inverse Matrix via Gaussian Elimination

The inverse of a square matrix A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n, denoted A−1A^{-1}A−1, is defined by the property

A⋅A−1=InA \cdot A^{-1} = I_nA⋅A−1=In​

where InI_nIn​ is the identity matrix of size n×nn \times nn×n.

This means that for every standard basis vector eje_jej​, we have

ej=Inej=A⋅(A−1ej).e_j = I_n e_j = A \cdot (A^{-1} e_j).ej​=In​ej​=A⋅(A−1ej​).

If we denote the jjj-th column of the inverse matrix A−1A^{-1}A−1 by vjv_jvj​, i.e.

vj=(A−1)⋅,j,v_j = (A^{-1})_{\cdot, j},vj​=(A−1)⋅,j​,

then each column satisfies a linear system:

Avj=ej.A v_j = e_j.Avj​=ej​.

Thus, computing the inverse matrix is equivalent to solving nnn linear systems simultaneously.

Gauss’ Algorithm

Instead of solving each system separately, we construct an augmented matrix:

(A∣In)(A \mid I_n)(A∣In​)

where the identity matrix is appended to the right side of AAA.

We then apply row operations to transform the left block AAA into reduced row echelon form.

If the matrix has full rank (i.e. it contains nnn pivot elements), the left block can be transformed into:

InI_nIn​

During the same row operations, the right block is transformed accordingly. At the end, we obtain:

(In∣A−1)(I_n \mid A^{-1})(In​∣A−1)

If fewer than nnn pivots appear during elimination, then rank(A)<n\mathrm{rank}(A) < nrank(A)<n and the inverse does not exist.

Let A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n be a square matrix. The inverse matrix A−1A^{-1}A−1 (if it exists) is defined by:

A⋅A−1=InA \cdot A^{-1} = I_nA⋅A−1=In​

This means each column of the inverse satisfies a linear system. If we denote the jjj-th column of A−1A^{-1}A−1 by vjv_jvj​, then:

Avj=ejA v_j = e_jAvj​=ej​

where eje_jej​ is the jjj-th standard basis vector.

Thus, computing the inverse is equivalent to solving nnn systems:

Av1=e1,Av2=e2,…,Avn=enA v_1 = e_1,\quad A v_2 = e_2,\quad \dots,\quad A v_n = e_nAv1​=e1​,Av2​=e2​,…,Avn​=en​

Instead of solving them separately, we solve them simultaneously using Gaussian elimination.

We construct the augmented matrix:

(A∣In)(A \mid I_n)(A∣In​)

This means we attach the identity matrix to the right side of AAA.

We then apply elementary row operations:

  • swapping two rows
  • multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar
  • adding a multiple of one row to another

These operations do not change the solution structure of the system.

The goal is to transform the left side into the identity matrix:

A⟶InA \longrightarrow I_nA⟶In​

If this is possible, the matrix is invertible. If not, then the matrix has insufficient pivot elements:

rank(A)<n⇒A−1 does not exist\mathrm{rank}(A) < n \quad \Rightarrow \quad A^{-1} \text{ does not exist}rank(A)<n⇒A−1 does not exist

If the process succeeds, the augmented matrix becomes:

(A∣In)⟶(In∣A−1)(A \mid I_n) \longrightarrow (I_n \mid A^{-1})(A∣In​)⟶(In​∣A−1)

Chapter 3: Rank, Invertability, Transposition of Matrices

Published: Wed, 3 Jun 2026 Revision: Wed, 3 Jun 2026, v 0.1 Language: This content is in English.

Definition: Row rank and column rank of a matrix

Let A∈Km×nA \in K^{m \times n}A∈Km×n be a matrix over a field KKK (for example K=RK = \mathbb{R}K=R or K=CK = \mathbb{C}K=C).

We associate to AAA several important subspaces: the row space, the column space, the kernel, and the image.

a) Row space

The row space of AAA is the subspace of KnK^nKn spanned by the rows of AAA (viewed as vectors in KnK^nKn):

Zeilenraum

ZR(A)=span({(A1,⋅)T,(A2,⋅)T,…,(Am,⋅)T})⊂Kn.ZR(A) = \text{span}\left(\{(A_{1,\cdot})^T, (A_{2,\cdot})^T, \ldots, (A_{m,\cdot})^T\}\right) \subset K^n.ZR(A)=span({(A1,⋅​)T,(A2,⋅​)T,…,(Am,⋅​)T})⊂Kn.
  • Each row of AAA is a vector with nnn components.
  • We take all rows and form all possible linear combinations.
  • The result is a subspace of KnK^nKn.

The row rank is the dimension of this space:

rang⁡Z(A)=dim⁡(ZR(A)).\operatorname{rang}_Z(A) = \dim(ZR(A)).rangZ​(A)=dim(ZR(A)).

b) Column space

The column space of AAA is the subspace of KmK^mKm spanned by the columns of AAA:

Spaltenraum

SR(A)=span({A⋅,1,A⋅,2,…,A⋅,n})⊂Km.SR(A) = \text{span}\left(\{A_{\cdot,1}, A_{\cdot,2}, \ldots, A_{\cdot,n}\}\right) \subset K^m.SR(A)=span({A⋅,1​,A⋅,2​,…,A⋅,n​})⊂Km.
  • Each column of AAA is a vector in KmK^mKm.
  • We take all columns and form all linear combinations.
  • The result is a subspace of KmK^mKm.

The column rank is:

rang⁡S(A)=dim⁡(SR(A)).\operatorname{rang}_S(A) = \dim(SR(A)).rangS​(A)=dim(SR(A)).

Key fact (important intuition)

For every matrix AAA:

rang⁡Z(A)=rang⁡S(A)\operatorname{rang}_Z(A) = \operatorname{rang}_S(A)rangZ​(A)=rangS​(A)

So we usually just call this number the rank of AAA.

c) Kernel

The kernel (null space) of AAA is:

ker⁡(A)={x∈Kn:Ax=0}.\ker(A) = \{x \in K^n : Ax = 0\}.ker(A)={x∈Kn:Ax=0}.

Interpretation:

  • These are all input vectors that get mapped to zero.
  • It measures how much information is “lost” under multiplication by AAA.

d) Image

The image (range) of AAA is:

im⁡(A)={Ax:x∈Kn}⊂Km.\operatorname{im}(A) = \{Ax : x \in K^n\} \subset K^m.im(A)={Ax:x∈Kn}⊂Km.

Interpretation:

  • All vectors in KmK^mKm that can actually be produced by applying AAA to some input vector.

Example

Consider the matrix:

A=(123246)∈R2×3.A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}.A=(12​24​36​)∈R2×3.

Row space

Rows are:

  • r1=(1,2,3)r_1 = (1,2,3)r1​=(1,2,3)
  • r2=(2,4,6)=2r1r_2 = (2,4,6) = 2r_1r2​=(2,4,6)=2r1​

So the second row is dependent.

Thus:

  • Row space is spanned only by (1,2,3)(1,2,3)(1,2,3)
  • So
rang⁡Z(A)=1.\operatorname{rang}_Z(A) = 1.rangZ​(A)=1.

Column space

Columns are:

c1=(12),c2=(24),c3=(36)c_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad c_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}, \quad c_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}c1​=(12​),c2​=(24​),c3​=(36​)

We see:

  • c2=2c1c_2 = 2c_1c2​=2c1​
  • c3=3c1c_3 = 3c_1c3​=3c1​

So all columns lie on a single line in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2.

Thus:

rang⁡S(A)=1.\operatorname{rang}_S(A) = 1.rangS​(A)=1.

Kernel

Solve Ax=0Ax = 0Ax=0:

Let x=(x1,x2,x3)Tx = (x_1, x_2, x_3)^Tx=(x1​,x2​,x3​)T.

Then:

x1+2x2+3x3=0x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 0x1​+2x2​+3x3​=0

So:

  • two free variables
  • kernel is a 2-dimensional subspace

Thus:

dim⁡(ker⁡(A))=2.\dim(\ker(A)) = 2.dim(ker(A))=2.

Image

The image is all multiples of:

(12)\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}(12​)

So:

dim⁡(im⁡(A))=1.\dim(\operatorname{im}(A)) = 1.dim(im(A))=1.

Intuition summary

  • Row space: what linear constraints exist between columns
  • Column space: what outputs are reachable
  • Kernel: what inputs disappear
  • Rank: how many independent directions remain

Lemma: Rank–nullity theorem for matrices

Let A∈Km×nA \in K^{m \times n}A∈Km×n and let

TA:Kn→Km,x↦AxT_A : K^n \to K^m, \quad x \mapsto AxTA​:Kn→Km,x↦Ax

be the linear map associated with the matrix AAA.

Then the following statements hold:

(a) Nullity

The nullity (in German: Defekt) of TAT_ATA​ equals the dimension of the kernel of AAA:

def⁡(TA)=dim⁡(ker⁡(A)).\operatorname{def}(T_A) = \dim(\ker(A)).def(TA​)=dim(ker(A)).

Interpretation:

  • The nullity measures how many independent directions are sent to zero.
  • It is exactly the dimension of the solution space of Ax=0Ax = 0Ax=0.

(b) Rank and column space

The rank of the linear map TAT_ATA​ equals the column rank of AAA:

rang⁡(TA)=rang⁡S(A).\operatorname{rang}(T_A) = \operatorname{rang}_S(A).rang(TA​)=rangS​(A).

Moreover,

rang⁡S(A)=n−dim⁡(ker⁡(A)).\operatorname{rang}_S(A) = n - \dim(\ker(A)).rangS​(A)=n−dim(ker(A)).

Proof

Step 1: Image of TAT_ATA​

By definition,

im⁡(TA)={Ax∣x∈Kn}.\operatorname{im}(T_A) = \{Ax \mid x \in K^n\}.im(TA​)={Ax∣x∈Kn}.

Step 2: Write AAA in terms of its columns

Let

A=(a1,a2,…,an)A = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)A=(a1​,a2​,…,an​)

where each ai∈Kma_i \in K^mai​∈Km is a column vector.

For x=(x1,…,xn)T∈Knx = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)^T \in K^nx=(x1​,…,xn​)T∈Kn, we compute:

Ax=x1a1+x2a2+⋯+xnan.Ax = x_1 a_1 + x_2 a_2 + \cdots + x_n a_n.Ax=x1​a1​+x2​a2​+⋯+xn​an​.

Interpretation:

  • Matrix multiplication is exactly forming a linear combination of the columns of AAA.

Step 3: Image = column space

From the above representation it follows that:

im⁡(TA)=span(a1,…,an)=SR(A).\operatorname{im}(T_A) = \text{span}(a_1, \ldots, a_n) = SR(A).im(TA​)=span(a1​,…,an​)=SR(A).

So:

  • the image of TAT_ATA​ is exactly the Spaltenraum (column space) of AAA.

Step 4: Rank equality

By definition of rank of a linear map:

rang⁡(TA)=dim⁡(im⁡(TA)).\operatorname{rang}(T_A) = \dim(\operatorname{im}(T_A)).rang(TA​)=dim(im(TA​)).

Thus:

rang⁡(TA)=dim⁡(SR(A))=rang⁡S(A).\operatorname{rang}(T_A) = \dim(SR(A)) = \operatorname{rang}_S(A).rang(TA​)=dim(SR(A))=rangS​(A).

Step 5: Dimension theorem (rank–nullity)

From the Dimensionssatz (rank–nullity theorem) for linear maps:

n=rang⁡(TA)+def⁡(TA).n = \operatorname{rang}(T_A) + \operatorname{def}(T_A).n=rang(TA​)+def(TA​).

Substituting (a):

n=rang⁡(TA)+dim⁡(ker⁡(A)).n = \operatorname{rang}(T_A) + \dim(\ker(A)).n=rang(TA​)+dim(ker(A)).

Rearranging:

rang⁡(TA)=n−dim⁡(ker⁡(A)).\operatorname{rang}(T_A) = n - \dim(\ker(A)).rang(TA​)=n−dim(ker(A)).

This lemma shows three equivalent ways to measure the “effective dimension” of a matrix:

  • Column rank: rang⁡S(A)\operatorname{rang}_S(A)rangS​(A)
  • Image dimension: dim⁡(im⁡(TA))\dim(\operatorname{im}(T_A))dim(im(TA​))
  • Kernel relation: n−dim⁡(ker⁡(A))n - \dim(\ker(A))n−dim(ker(A))

All of them describe the same quantity: the number of independent directions that survive after applying AAA.

Theorem: Equality of row rank and column rank

Let A∈Km×nA \in K^{m \times n}A∈Km×n.

Then

rang⁡Z(A)=rang⁡S(A).\operatorname{rang}_Z(A) = \operatorname{rang}_S(A).rangZ​(A)=rangS​(A).

Recall:

  • The Zeilenrang (row rank) is the dimension of the row space.
  • The Spaltenrang (column rank) is the dimension of the column space.

This theorem states that these two numbers are always equal.

Because of this result, we can simply speak of the rank of a matrix.

Why is this true?

From the lemma we know:

rang⁡S(A)=n−dim⁡(ker⁡(A)).\operatorname{rang}_S(A) = n - \dim(\ker(A)).rangS​(A)=n−dim(ker(A)).

Applying the same argument to the transpose ATA^TAT gives

rang⁡S(AT)=m−dim⁡(ker⁡(AT)).\operatorname{rang}_S(A^T) = m - \dim(\ker(A^T)).rangS​(AT)=m−dim(ker(AT)).

But:

  • The columns of ATA^TAT are the rows of AAA.
  • Therefore
rang⁡S(AT)=rang⁡Z(A).\operatorname{rang}_S(A^T) = \operatorname{rang}_Z(A).rangS​(AT)=rangZ​(A).

Corollary: Upper Bound for the Rank

For every matrix A∈Km×nA \in K^{m \times n}A∈Km×n,

rang⁡Z(A)=rang⁡S(A)≤min⁡(m,n).\operatorname{rang}_Z(A) = \operatorname{rang}_S(A) \leq \min(m,n).rangZ​(A)=rangS​(A)≤min(m,n).

Explanation

A matrix has:

  • mmm rows,
  • nnn columns.

Since there cannot be more linearly independent rows than rows themselves,

rang⁡(A)≤m.\operatorname{rang}(A) \leq m.rang(A)≤m.

Likewise,

rang⁡(A)≤n.\operatorname{rang}(A) \leq n.rang(A)≤n.

Combining both inequalities yields

rang⁡(A)≤min⁡(m,n).\operatorname{rang}(A) \leq \min(m,n).rang(A)≤min(m,n).

Thus the rank can never exceed the smaller of the two dimensions.

Definition: Rank and Regular Matrices

Because of Theorem, row rank and column rank coincide.

Therefore we define the rank (Rang) of a matrix A∈Km×nA \in K^{m \times n}A∈Km×n by

rang⁡(A)=rang⁡Z(A)=rang⁡S(A).\operatorname{rang}(A) = \operatorname{rang}_Z(A) = \operatorname{rang}_S(A).rang(A)=rangZ​(A)=rangS​(A).

A matrix is called regular (regulär) if its rank is as large as possible:

rang⁡(A)=min⁡(m,n).\operatorname{rang}(A) = \min(m,n).rang(A)=min(m,n).

In other words, a regular matrix has the maximum possible number of linearly independent rows and columns.

Examples

Regular:

(1001)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}(10​01​)

since

rang⁡(A)=2=min⁡(2,2).\operatorname{rang}(A)=2=\min(2,2).rang(A)=2=min(2,2).

Not regular:

(1224)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}(12​24​)

since

rang⁡(A)=1<2.\operatorname{rang}(A)=1<2.rang(A)=1<2.

Corollary: Invertibility Criterion

A matrix

A∈Km×nA \in K^{m \times n}A∈Km×n

is invertible if and only if

  1. AAA is square:

    m=n,m=n,m=n,

  2. AAA is regular:

    rang⁡(A)=n.\operatorname{rang}(A)=n.rang(A)=n.

Equivalently,

A invertible  ⟺  A∈Kn×n and rang⁡(A)=n.A \text{ invertible} \iff A \in K^{n \times n} \text{ and } \operatorname{rang}(A)=n.A invertible⟺A∈Kn×n and rang(A)=n.

Proof

Use Lemma 2.17.

The associated linear map

TA:Kn→Kn,x↦AxT_A : K^n \to K^n, \qquad x \mapsto AxTA​:Kn→Kn,x↦Ax

is invertible if and only if it is bijective.

By the rank-nullity theorem,

n=rang⁡(A)+dim⁡(ker⁡(A)).n = \operatorname{rang}(A) + \dim(\ker(A)).n=rang(A)+dim(ker(A)).

A bijective map must have trivial kernel:

ker⁡(A)={0}.\ker(A)=\{0\}.ker(A)={0}.

Hence

dim⁡(ker⁡(A))=0,\dim(\ker(A))=0,dim(ker(A))=0,

which implies

rang⁡(A)=n.\operatorname{rang}(A)=n.rang(A)=n.

Therefore a square matrix is invertible precisely when it has full rank.

Definition: Transpose of a Matrix

Let

A∈Km×n.A \in K^{m \times n}.A∈Km×n.

The transpose (transponierte Matrix) of AAA is the matrix

AT∈Kn×mA^T \in K^{n \times m}AT∈Kn×m

defined by

AT(i,j)=A(j,i)A^T(i,j)=A(j,i)AT(i,j)=A(j,i)

for all

i∈{1,…,n},j∈{1,…,m}.i \in \{1,\dots,n\}, \qquad j \in \{1,\dots,m\}.i∈{1,…,n},j∈{1,…,m}.

The transpose is obtained by exchanging rows and columns.

Every row of AAA becomes a column of ATA^TAT and every column of AAA becomes a row of ATA^TAT.

Example

If

A=(123456),A= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{pmatrix},A=(14​25​36​),

then

AT=(142536).A^T= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 \end{pmatrix}.AT=​123​456​​.

The first row (1,2,3)(1,2,3)(1,2,3) becomes the first column, and the second row (4,5,6)(4,5,6)(4,5,6) becomes the second column.

Important Properties

(AT)T=A(A^T)^T = A(AT)T=A (A+B)T=AT+BT(A+B)^T = A^T + B^T(A+B)T=AT+BT (λA)T=λAT(\lambda A)^T = \lambda A^T(λA)T=λAT (AB)T=BTAT(AB)^T = B^T A^T(AB)T=BTAT

The last identity is especially important because the order of multiplication reverses when taking the transpose.

Lemma: Properties of the Transpose

Let

A,B∈Km×nA,B \in K^{m \times n}A,B∈Km×n

and

C∈Kk×m.C \in K^{k \times m}.C∈Kk×m.

Then the following properties hold.

(a) Double Transpose

(AT)T=A.(A^T)^T = A.(AT)T=A.

Explanation

Transposition exchanges rows and columns.

Applying the transpose once swaps rows and columns.

Applying it a second time swaps them back, recovering the original matrix.

Example

A=(123456)A= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{pmatrix}A=(14​25​36​)

First transpose:

AT=(142536)A^T= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 \end{pmatrix}AT=​123​456​​

Transposing again:

(AT)T=(123456)=A.(A^T)^T= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{pmatrix} =A.(AT)T=(14​25​36​)=A.

(b) Transpose of a Sum

(A+B)T=AT+BT.(A+B)^T = A^T + B^T.(A+B)T=AT+BT.

Explanation

The transpose acts entry-wise:

(A+B)ij=Aij+Bij.(A+B)_{ij} = A_{ij}+B_{ij}.(A+B)ij​=Aij​+Bij​.

Swapping indices gives

(A+B)ijT=Aji+Bji=(AT+BT)ij.(A+B)^T_{ij} = A_{ji}+B_{ji} = (A^T+ B^T)_{ij}.(A+B)ijT​=Aji​+Bji​=(AT+BT)ij​.

Thus transposition distributes over addition.

(c) Transpose of a Product

(CA)T=ATCT.(CA)^T = A^T C^T.(CA)T=ATCT.

Important

The order of multiplication is reversed.

This is one of the most frequently used transpose identities.

Notice carefully:

(CA)T≠CTAT(CA)^T \neq C^T A^T(CA)T=CTAT

in general.

The factors switch places.

Example

If

CA=(abcd),CA= \begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d \end{pmatrix},CA=(ac​bd​),

then

(CA)T=(acbd),(CA)^T = \begin{pmatrix} a & c\\ b & d \end{pmatrix},(CA)T=(ab​cd​),

which coincides with

ATCT.A^T C^T.ATCT.

(d) Transpose of an Inverse

Suppose

A∈Kn×nA \in K^{n \times n}A∈Kn×n

is invertible.

Then

(AT)−1=(A−1)T.(A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T.(AT)−1=(A−1)T.

Consequently,

ATA^TAT

is also invertible.

Reason

Using part (c),

AT(A−1)T=(A−1A)T.A^T (A^{-1})^T = (A^{-1}A)^T.AT(A−1)T=(A−1A)T.

Since

A−1A=I,A^{-1}A=I,A−1A=I,

we obtain

(A−1A)T=IT=I.(A^{-1}A)^T = I^T = I.(A−1A)T=IT=I.

Likewise,

(A−1)TAT=I.(A^{-1})^T A^T = I.(A−1)TAT=I.

Therefore

(A−1)T(A^{-1})^T(A−1)T

is the inverse of

AT.A^T.AT.

Definition: Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices

Let

A∈Kn×nA \in K^{n \times n}A∈Kn×n

be a square matrix.

(a) Symmetric Matrix (symmetrische Matrix)

A matrix is called symmetric if

AT=A.A^T = A.AT=A.

In a symmetric matrix, the entries above and below the main diagonal are mirror images of each other:

aij=aji.a_{ij}=a_{ji}.aij​=aji​.

Example

(123245356)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 5 \\ 3 & 5 & 6 \end{pmatrix}​123​245​356​​

is symmetric.

(b) Skew-Symmetric Matrix (schiefsymmetrische Matrix)

A matrix is called skew-symmetric if

AT=−A.A^T = -A.AT=−A.

Equivalently,

aij=−aji.a_{ij}=-a_{ji}.aij​=−aji​.

A consequence is that every diagonal entry must satisfy

aii=−aii,a_{ii}=-a_{ii},aii​=−aii​,

hence

aii=0a_{ii}=0aii​=0

(over fields where 2≠02 \neq 02=0, such as R\mathbb{R}R).

Example

(02−1−2041−40)\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}​0−21​20−4​−140​​

is skew-symmetric.

Remark: Decomposition into Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Parts

Every square matrix

A∈Kn×nA \in K^{n \times n}A∈Kn×n

can be written as the sum of

  • a symmetric matrix,
  • a skew-symmetric matrix.

Specifically,

A=12(A+AT)+12(A−AT).A = \frac{1}{2}(A+A^T) + \frac{1}{2}(A-A^T).A=21​(A+AT)+21​(A−AT).

Let

S=12(A+AT),S=\frac{1}{2}(A+A^T),S=21​(A+AT),

and

K=12(A−AT).K=\frac{1}{2}(A-A^T).K=21​(A−AT).

Then

A=S+K.A=S+K.A=S+K.

Why is SSS symmetric?

Taking the transpose:

ST=12(A+AT)T=12(AT+A)=S.S^T = \frac{1}{2}(A+A^T)^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T+A) = S.ST=21​(A+AT)T=21​(AT+A)=S.

Thus SSS is symmetric.

Why is KKK skew-symmetric?

Taking the transpose:

KT=12(A−AT)T=12(AT−A)=−K.K^T = \frac{1}{2}(A-A^T)^T = \frac{1}{2}(A^T-A) = -K.KT=21​(A−AT)T=21​(AT−A)=−K.

Thus KKK is skew-symmetric.

Example

Let

A=(1324).A= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}.A=(12​34​).

Then

AT=(1234).A^T= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}.AT=(13​24​).

Symmetric part:

12(A+AT)=12(2558)=(12.52.54).\frac{1}{2}(A+A^T) = \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 5 & 8 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2.5 \\ 2.5 & 4 \end{pmatrix}.21​(A+AT)=21​(25​58​)=(12.5​2.54​).

Skew-symmetric part:

12(A−AT)=12(01−10)=(00.5−0.50).\frac{1}{2}(A-A^T) = \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0.5 \\ -0.5 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.21​(A−AT)=21​(0−1​10​)=(0−0.5​0.50​).

Adding both matrices recovers AAA.

Uniqueness

The decomposition

A=12(A+AT)+12(A−AT)A = \frac{1}{2}(A+A^T) + \frac{1}{2}(A-A^T)A=21​(A+AT)+21​(A−AT)

is unique.

That means there is exactly one symmetric matrix and exactly one skew-symmetric matrix whose sum equals AAA.

This is analogous to writing a vector as the sum of components in two independent directions.
